title: Mastercard Launches Their Own Stablecoin Platform
description: Mastercard Bought BVNK. Two Months Later, It Launched a Stablecoin Platform.
coverAlt: Mastercard Launched a Stablecoin Platform by VAK Marketing
seoTitle: Mastercard Launches Their Own Stablecoin Platform
html:
On October 15, Mastercard and BVNK unveiled Global Money Platform, their first major product integration since Mastercard acquired the stablecoin infrastructure company in August.


 The platform allows banks, fintechs and businesses to offer accounts holding both traditional currencies and stablecoins through a single API. It also brings together real-time currency conversion, stablecoin-linked cards and local bank payouts through Mastercard Move. Nuvei and Marqeta are among the first companies preparing to integrate the service. The interesting part is what happens after a business receives stablecoins. A company might accept payments on-chain, but its suppliers still expect transfers to local bank accounts, and customers need familiar ways to spend their money. Connecting these processes through existing payment infrastructure could remove some of the complications businesses face when moving funds between traditional banking and blockchain networks.

Mastercard says the platform is available through BVNK now, which was acquired by the former, with broader local payout coverage planned for 2027. For payment providers, the announcement also raises the bar for how stablecoin services are marketed. "Fast global payments" tells a prospective client very little about the actual offering. Supported currencies, payout destinations, settlement arrangements and integration requirements are the details that matter when a business starts comparing providers.  

FAQ

What does the Global Money Platform actually do?

It brings four capabilities behind one API: multi-currency accounts holding fiat and stablecoins together with configurable rewards, real-time conversion between them, stablecoin-linked cards spendable across Mastercard’s acceptance network with issuing capability in more than 130 countries and territories, and payouts that turn stablecoin balances into local-currency credits to bank accounts through Mastercard Move and its 17 billion-plus endpoints. Banks, fintechs and enterprises can white-label it or use it internally for treasury and settlement.

What does a merchant receive when someone pays with stablecoins?

Local fiat currency, with no exposure to crypto at any point. Conversion happens at authorization between the cardholder and the issuer, priced at a live rate plus the card program’s spread, with the balance locked and the rate fixed at that moment. The transaction then clears through the card network in fiat, the acquirer is credited in local currency, the issuer is debited in fiat, and the locked stablecoin is debited on the cardholder side during reconciliation.

How long does a stablecoin payout to a bank account take?

The on-chain leg can complete in seconds, but final crediting depends on the recipient country’s local clearing system and banking hours rather than on block confirmation speed. The path runs through Mastercard Move, whose advantage is bypassing the correspondent banking chain and the time and cost it adds. Coverage is expected to reach more than 40 currencies across 200-plus countries and territories in 2027, so today’s footprint is smaller than that target.

Are stablecoin payments genuinely cheaper?

It depends on the corridor. Using the typical ranges from industry research, conversion spreads run from zero to 2.49% with USDC and USDT spending usually free of conversion fees, cross-border markup runs from zero to 1.5% against the 1% to 3% banks commonly charge, issuing fees run from zero to $20 a month against zero to $10 for traditional debit, and merchant interchange is identical because the rails are the same. The advantage is clear cross-border and close to absent for everyday domestic spending.

Which fee is easiest to miss?

The conversion spread. It never appears as a separate line, because it is baked into the rate locked at authorization, so the user sees an executed rate without seeing how far above mid-market it sits. Comparing published fee tables therefore tells you little. Running the same amount through two products and comparing the final credited or debited figure is the reliable test. Network fees add a second variable, since they move with chain congestion.

What are the current limitations?

The announcement names no specific stablecoins, so supported assets depend on each integrator’s setup and on local regulation. Issuing capability across 130-plus countries describes network reach, not that residents in all of them can open a card today. Agentic commerce support and tokenised deposits remain on the roadmap. US rules also bar permitted issuers from paying interest to holders while platform-level rewards remain unlegislated, so the configurable rewards described will not be uniformly available across jurisdictions.
